title: Hysteroscopic metroplasty and its reproductive impact among the social networks: A cross-sectional analysis on video quality, reliability and creators' opinions on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of 115 social-media videos on hysteroscopic metroplasty. Every video was fact-checked against accepted hysteroscopy guidelines and the existing literature and classified by the proportion of false information it carried ('inaccurate or misinformative' = >50 % false information). Platform-level shares of videos falling in the inaccurate category are reported verbatim (YouTube 8.5 %, TikTok 42.9 %, Instagram 36.4 %), so the paper gives quantitative shares of items classified false against an external ground truth (CONTENT). The parallel PEMAT A/V, mDISCERN, GQS and VIQI instruments are quality scores reported only as medians (IQR) and yield no share, so they produce no rows.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language videos from creators worldwide; authors based in Italy)
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube videos on hysteroscopic metroplasty classified 'inaccurate or uninformative' (>50 % false information)
estimates.denominator: 47 YouTube videos on hysteroscopy / uterine septum included from the first 300 retrieved on that platform
estimates.definition: video judged, after fact-checking against accepted hysteroscopy guidelines and the existing literature, to contain more than 50 % false information
estimates.misinfo_def: content with more than 50 % false information was classified as "inaccurate or misinformative"; videos with less than 50 % but more than 25 % false information were classified as "partially accurate"; videos with less than 25 % misinformation were labeled as "accurate and evidence-based"
estimates.source_quote: Concerning the misinformation about hysteroscopic septum resec- tion, most of the content was considered accurate (evidence-based or partially accurate) in most of the videos on social networks. However, there were significant differences among the platforms, as videos were categorized as Inaccurate or uninformative for 42.9 % and 36.4 % in TikTok and Instagram respectively, compared to the 8.5 % reported for YouTube ( Table 2 ; p = 0.001).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: One senior gynecologist (>500 hysteroscopic procedures) and two OB/GYN residents independently and simultaneously scored every video against accepted hysteroscopy guidelines and existing literature; discrepancies were resolved by a fourth gynecologist to consensus. No inter-rater reliability statistic (kappa or similar) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: Each video underwent a rigorous fact-checking process to identify and correct any erroneous information presented. This verification was conducted using accepted guidelines for hysteroscopy and data from existing literature.
estimates.notes: Search keywords 'hysteroscopy' + 'septate uterus' or 'uterine septum'; a fresh account was created to limit algorithmic personalisation; only the first 300 videos per platform were screened, hence denom_selection=curated. The Table 2 label reads 'Inaccurate or uninformative' while the Methods label is 'inaccurate or misinformative' — the operational definition in Methods is purely falsity-based (>50 % false information), which is why this is coded CONTENT rather than QUALITY; an adjudicator should note the label drift. The three 'partially accurate' shares are not extracted as separate rows and no accurate+partially-accurate or partially+inaccurate sum was computed (R8).

missed_or_uncertain: (1) No pooled across-platform share of inaccurate videos is stated for the 115-video corpus, so none was computed (R8 forbids cross-category/cross-platform sums). (2) The 'partially accurate' category (25-50 % false information) is reported per platform (YouTube 19/47 implied, TikTok 6 (17.1), Instagram 12 (36.4)) but the OCR of Table 2 is garbled and two of the nine accuracy cells are missing from the text, so only the three verbatim 'inaccurate' shares in Section 3.2 and the abstract were extracted; a broader 'any false information' share would require summing categories, which R8 forbids. (3) PEMAT A/V Understandability/Actionability, mDISCERN, GQS and VIQI are reported only as medians with IQR and ranges; mDISCERN >= 3 and GQS >= 3 are described as thresholds for 'highly reliable' and 'high-quality', but the paper never reports the share of videos above those thresholds, so no QUALITY row could be made (a Likert/scale instrument reported only as a median is not a share). (4) Stance items ('in favor of hysteroscopic metroplasty' 97.9 % YouTube, 62.9 % TikTok; 'improves reproductive outcomes' 82.9 %/57.1 %/63.6 %) are opinions about a contested procedure, not falsity codings against a ground truth, so they were not extracted as prevalence estimates.

rob.design: Cross-sectional platform content analysis. Frame: the first 300 videos returned per platform (YouTube, TikTok, Instagram) on 30 March 2024 for 'hysteroscopy' plus 'septate uterus'/'uterine septum', searched from a newly created account to limit personalisation; 900 screened, 785 excluded (601 off-topic, 147 non-English, 1 removed, 37 duplicates), 115 analysed (47/35/33). Coding: one senior gynecologist and two OB/GYN residents independently and simultaneously scored each video with PEMAT A/V, mDISCERN, GQS, VIQI and a misinformation category fact-checked against hysteroscopy guidelines; discrepancies adjudicated by a fourth gynecologist to consensus. No inter-rater reliability statistic reported; no response-rate concept (non-human data); IRB approval waived.
rob.item6_quote: The level of misinformation in the videos was categorized as follows: content with more than 50 % false information was classified as " inaccurate or misinformative " ; videos with less than 50 % but more than 25 % false information were classified as " partially ac-curate " ; videos with less than 25 % misinformation were labeled as " accurate and evidence-based. rob.item10_quote: One hundred fifteen videos (47 from YouTube, 35 from TikTok, and 33 from Instagram) were included. ... significant differences in misinformation levels were observed across platforms, with YouTube exhibiting the lowest rate of inaccuracies compared to TikTok and Instagram.
